section.title: Children's Safeguards Review
section.p: Dr. Godman: To ask the Secretary of State for Scotland when he intends announcing the Government's response to the Children's Safeguard Review prepared by Roger Kent; and if he will make a statement. [58947]

Mr. Dewar: Action is being taken on a number of fronts to safeguard and promote the welfare of children living away from home. Today I am pleased to announce that the Government's response to Mr. Kent's Review has been made available in the Libraries of both Houses. We consulted widely on the Review and its 61 recommendations. We see it as an important milestone in raising standards and improving services for looked after children. Our response demonstrates our practical commitment to this process and sets out priorities for action. That commitment will be underpinned by resources.

I can announce today that an additional £36.7m over the next 3 years will be made available to improve children's services, £15m of which will be allocated specifically for implementation of key proposals in the Review. The Government's response, supported by
635 additional resources, is a clear indication of the importance we attach to this task. It will be made widely available to local authorities and voluntary organisations so that they can play their full part in helping to protect and secure better outcomes for this vulnerable group. We owe them nothing less.

section.title: Food-related Scientific Services
section.p: Mr. Jim Murphy: To ask the Secretary of State for Scotland when the independent group appointed in May to undertake a review of food-related scientific services in Scotland is due to report. [58950]

Mr. Galbraith: The Review Group led by Professor Morag Timbury provided me with their final report on 23 October and copies are available in the House of Commons Library. I am very grateful to the Chairman and Members of the Group for undertaking this complex review of a service which is an essential element of the food law enforcement and surveillance system which directly helps to safeguard public health. The detailed recommendations presented by the Group will be very carefully considered in order to ensure that all necessary changes to the existing system can be introduced to secure an efficient and effective food-related scientific service.

section.title: Senator Pinochet
section.p: Mr. Forth: To ask the Secretary of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs what arrangements were made by or through his Department for the arrival of Senator Pinochet in the United Kingdom. [57042]
Mr. Tony Lloyd: I refer the right hon. Member to the answer I gave to the hon. Member for Spelthorne (Mr. Wilshire) on 4 November 1998, Official Report, column 601.

Mr. Howard: To ask the Secretary of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs if he will list all representations and telephone calls made by his Department about Senator Pinochet between 14 and 17 October; and to whom they were made. [57966]

Mr. Tony Lloyd [holding answer 2 November 1998]: This Department made no representations and does not keep comprehensive records of telephone calls. But there were a number of calls with the relevant authorities at the time of his arrest, and my right hon. Friend the Foreign Secretary received a telephone call from the Chilean Foreign Minister on 17 October.

Mr. Wilshire: To ask the Secretary of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs, pursuant to his answer to the hon. Member for Walsall, North (Mr. Winnick) of 22 October 1998, Official Report, column 1206, and to the answer given to the hon. Member for Hertsmere (Mr. Clappison) of 27 October 1998, Official Report, column 124, if he will list the precise dates on which Senator Pinochet has been in the United Kingdom since 1 May 1997. [57659]

Mr. Tony Lloyd [holding answer 2 November 1998]: Pursuant to an answer given by my right hon. Friend the 636 Secretary of State for the Home Department to the hon. Member for Hertsmere (Mr. Clappison) on 27 October 1998, Official Report, column 124, our records indicate that Senator Pinochet arrived in the United Kingdom on 29 September 1997 and left on 21 October 1997, with a break abroad between 5–17 October. He arrived in London on his current visit on 22 September 1998.

Mr. Howard: To ask the Secretary of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs what communications his Department received from the Embassy in Chile in the week prior to the arrest of Senator Pinochet. [58417]

Mr. Tony Lloyd: On 9 October, the Embassy inquired about Senator Pinochet's health and whereabouts following press inquiries it had received that he had died that afternoon in London. The Embassy afterwards faxed a note of this incident for the record to London. On 16 October, the Embassy commented on reports of Spanish judicial moves against Senator Pinochet.

section.title: Gibraltar
section.p: Mr. Mackinlay: To ask the Secretary of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs what initiatives were rejected during the United Kingdom presidency of the EU by Spain consequent to the dispute over the status of Gibraltar. [55981]

Ms Quin [pursuant to her reply, 26 October 1998, c. 86]: An administrative error led to an incorrect reference to the number of instruments adopted at the Justice and Home Affairs Council on 28–29 May. A revised answer is printed below.

Before the start of the UK Presidency, Spain objected to various draft instruments in the Justice and Home Affairs field because of the terms relating to the inclusion of Gibraltar. We fully consulted the Government of Gibraltar throughout the ensuing negotiations during our Presidency. The Government of Gibraltar reluctantly decided that Gibraltar should be excluded from these instruments rather than participate as part of the UK legal jurisdiction. Two instruments were adopted at the Justice and Home Affairs Council on 28–29 May on this basis (ie with Gibraltar excluded): the Driving Disqualifications Convention and the European Judicial Network Joint Action. Gibraltar was excluded from a third measure at the JHA Council which has not yet been adopted (the Eurodac Convention).

section.title: Visitor Visas
section.p: Mr. Gerrard: To ask the Secretary of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs what information he collects regarding the numbers of people who, having been refused visit visas to enter the United Kingdom, have subsequently been granted visas as a result of a new application at a later date. [57334]
Mr. Fatchett: This Department does not record this information.

Mr. Hancock: To ask the Secretary of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs how many people, and from which countries, had visitors' visa applications rejected by UK officials in each of the last three years. [58286]

Mr. Fatchett: The number of visit visa applications (including short term students) refused at overseas Posts in the last three years is as follows:
Year Number
1995 65,209
1996 69,791
1997 60,019
Our statistics are recorded by country of application but do not show the country of origin of the applicant.

section.title: Antarctic Treaty Secretariat
section.p: Mr. Corbyn: To ask the Secretary of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs when he expects progress to be made on the establishment of an Antarctic Treaty Secretariat; and if he will make a statement. [58231]

Mr. Tony Lloyd: The Antarctic Treaty Secretariat may be discussed at the next meeting of the Antarctic Treaty Consultative Parties to be held in Peru in May 1999. The need for an Antarctic Treaty Secretariat has long been acknowledged by Consultative Parties, including the UK. But consensus on its location has not yet been reached.

section.title: Sierra Leone
section.p: Mr. Jim Cunningham: To ask the Secretary of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs what recent initiatives his Department has taken to resolve conflict in Sierra Leone. [57796]

Mr. Tony Lloyd: We are playing a leading role in helping to promote lasting peace, democracy and prosperity in Sierra Leone. Britain is hosting the first meeting of the Sierra Leone Contract Group on 5 November. The meeting is intended to boost the efforts of the International community to build peace and reconciliation in Sierra Leone. Britain is also helping to resolve conflict by supporting the disarmament and reintegration of ex-combatants, through a £6.5 million pledge from the Department for International Development.

section.title: International Forum for Federalism
section.p: Mr. Maclean: To ask the Secretary of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs if he will make a statement on the planned participation by representatives from (a) the United Kingdom and (b) European Communities institutions at the inaugural conference of an International Forum for Federalism to be held by the Canadian Government. [58276]

Mr. Tony Lloyd: We are aware that the Deputy Prime Minister of Canada suggested the idea of an International Forum for Federalism in a speech to the London School of Economics and Political Science on 29 October. However, it would not be appropriate for HMG to make a statement on this initiative which, we understand, is only at an early stage of development.

section.title: Tobacco (EU Aid)
section.p: Mr. Fearn: To ask the Secretary of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs what is the Government's policy on European Union aid to tobacco growers. [57182]
Mr. Rooker: I have been asked to reply.

The Government strongly disapprove of the Common Agricultural Policy support regime for tobacco. We believe that the Community should progressively disengage from support for tobacco production on grounds of health and cost. We continue to press for further progress in this area following the reform of the regime agreed in June of this year.

section.title: Waste Recycling
section.p: Mr. Bob Russell: To ask the Secretary of State for the Environment, Transport and the Regions what percentage of waste from the London boroughs of (a) Edmonton and (b) Lewisham is recycled. [56749]

Mr. Meale: Information from the Department's Municipal Waste Survey shows that the percentage of waste collected for recycling in 1996–97 in the London boroughs of Enfield (which includes Edmonton) and Lewisham were:
London borough Percentage
Enfield1 6.4
Lewisham 2.8
1Total waste includes amounts collected at North London Waste Authority civil amenity sites situated in the borough of Enfield. Waste collected for recycling includes material recovered through mechanised metal extraction.

section.title: Driving Test Centres
section.p: Mr. Kidney: To ask the Secretary of State for the Environment, Transport and the Regions, pursuant to his answer to the hon. Member for Crosby (Mrs. Curtis-Thomas) of 26 October 1998, Official Report, column 7, what plans the Driving Standards Agency has to re-establish a test centre in Stafford. [57486]
Ms Glenda Jackson: The Driving Standards Agency remains committed to re-establishing a driving test centre in Stafford. The search for a suitable site is continuing.

section.title: Genetically Modified Organisms
section.p: Mr. Alan Simpson: To ask the Secretary of State for the Environment, Transport and the Regions what plans he has to amend the remit of the Advisory Committee on Releases to the Environment; and what proposals for public participation in any decision relating to such changes he intends to make. [57412]

Mr. Meacher: The terms of reference for the Advisory Committee on Releases to the Environment already include the provision of advice on request to the Secretary of State. In future we shall be seeking advice from ACRE not only on the direct and indirect effects of genetically modified organisms into the environment but also on the possible resultant changes in agronomic practice and the subsequent effects on biodiversity. ACRE's advice on these questions will be made public through the DETR public register.

section.title: Recycled Land
section.p: Mr. Brake: To ask the Secretary of State for the Environment, Transport and the Regions, pursuant to his answer of 28 July 1998, Official Report, column 110, if he will publish the Oxford Brookes University research on the use of economic instruments to make it attractive to develop new housing on recycled land. [57928]

Mr. Raynsford: As part of the Modernising Planning initiative this year, Oxford Brookes University were commissioned to lead some seminars with stakeholders on the development of planning obligations, including the role of economic instruments, in connection with a wide range of development interests, including housing. The seminars were held under 'Chatham House' rules, with participants contributing under the assurance of confidentiality. Following the seminars Oxford Brookes University prepared a report to the Department with their findings. The Department is now considering these but has no plans to publish the report.

section.title: Jubilee Line
section.p: Mr. Gibb: To ask the Secretary of State for the Environment, Transport and the Regions how much Bechtel is charging per day to take over the project management of the Jubilee Line extension. [58202]
Ms Glenda Jackson: The contract between London Transport and Bechtel covers the provision of personnel with a structured charging mechanism, the details of which are commercially confidential.

section.title: Birmingham Northern Relief Road
section.p: Mr. Jenkins: To ask the Secretary of State for the Environment, Transport and the Regions what is the estimated start date of the Birmingham Northern Relief Road. [58108]
Ms Glenda Jackson: The start date is subject to the early determination of any appeal against the High Court judgment of 20 October on the statutory challenge to the orders for the scheme.

section.title: Kyoto Agreement
section.p: Mr. Nigel Jones: To ask the Secretary of State for the Environment, Transport and the Regions what assessment he has made of progress towards implementing the Kyoto agreement by (a) the United Kingdom, (b) other members of the European Union and (c) the United States of America. [57881]

Mr. Meale: On 26 October we became one of the first developed countries to launch a consultation paper on meeting its Kyoto commitments. The paper lists the steps we have already taken and sets out in detail further options on how the UK could reduce its emissions of greenhouse gases. It demonstrates that the UK is well placed to meet both its legally binding Kyoto target to cut greenhouse gas emissions to 12.5% below 1990 levels by 2008 to 2012 and our domestic aim of a 20% cut in CO2, emissions by 2010. Greenhouse gas emissions are already about 7% below 1990 levels; and, on current policies, would be about 10% below by 2010.

European Union Member States are required under the Council Decision for a monitoring mechanism of Community C02 and other greenhouse gas emissions to report annually on their emissions. The UK Government monitor these reports closely. This mechanism has now been amended to allow assessment of progress towards meeting Member States' Kyoto targets.

Through our Washington Embassy and other contacts I receive regular reports of action taken, and proposed, by the US Government to reduce their greenhouse gas emissions. A recent US Administration report ("The Kyoto Protocol and the President's Policies to Address Climate Change: Administration Economic Analysis", July 1998) assessing the economic implications of their Kyoto target concluded that there was a strong rationale for action because of the dangers of climate change, and that the costs of doing so were likely to be modest.

section.title: Great Barford Bypass
section.p: Sir Nicholas Lyell: To ask the Secretary of State for the Environment, Transport and the Regions when he expects to instruct the Highways Agency to appoint consultants in relation to the Great Barford Bypass. [58102]

Ms Glenda Jackson: This scheme is included in our Targeted Programme of Improvements listed in A New Deal for Trunk Roads in England. That means that the scheme will definitely start within the next seven years, subject only to any outstanding statutory procedures. Detailed decisions on the timing of the schemes in the programme will be made shortly.
In the light of these decisions, the appointment of consultants and design agents will be commissioned to meet the agreed programme.

section.title: Arco Arun
section.p: Mr. Mackinlay: To ask the Secretary of State for the Environment, Transport and the Regions if he will make a statement on the circumstances surrounding the sinking of the Arco Arum and subsequent salvage attempts in the Thames off Thurrock. [58077]

Ms Glenda Jackson: I believe my hon. Friend's question relates to the vessel Arco Arun. I understand that this aggregate dredger grounded off Broadness Point at approximately 1450 hours on 13 October. The vessel sustained a split in her hull and subsequently sank, clear of the navigation channel. No other vessels were involved, there were no casualties and, due to the quick response by the Port of London Authority, no damage to the environment. An inquiry by the Marine Accidents Investigation Branch is in progress and the PLA is conducting its own internal investigations. I understand that, following the appointment of salvors by the vessel owners, it became apparent that flooding had spread throughout the vessel and that specialist equipment would be required. The vessel owners have therefore now engaged the services of a company experienced in heavy lift and removal operations and they are currently assessing the situation.

section.title: Housing Associations
section.p:
Mr. Bob Russell: To ask the Secretary of State for the Environment, Transport and the Regions what procedures
641 exist for him to monitor housing associations; and if he will arrange for the operations of the Springboard Housing Association to be investigated. [58097]
Mr. Raynsford: The Housing Corporation has the statutory responsibility for registering, regulating and funding housing associations, now known as Registered Social Landlords.

Springboard Housing Association is registered with the Housing Corporation. The association, along with all other Registered Social Landlords, is required to meet the Housing Corporation's Performance Standards. Compliance with these standards is reviewed annually. The Corporation investigates where there is evidence of non-compliance and has powers to ensure remedial action by RSLs in cases of serious mismanagement or misconduct.
I have asked the Housing Corporation to contact the hon. Member direct to answer any specific concerns.

section.title: Millennium Experience (Cable Car)
section.p: Mr. Spring: To ask the Secretary of State for the Environment, Transport and the Regions if he will make a statement on the role of the cable car link to the Millennium Experience; and how many passengers it is expected to carry. [58018]

Ms Glenda Jackson: The Millennium Access transport strategy was developed before the proposed cable car, being promoted by a private company, was a consideration. The New Millennium Experience Company has estimated that 2 per cent. of visitors would use the cable car for part of their journey to the Dome. Should it not proceed there would be sufficient capacity on other modes to carry visitors to the Dome who might otherwise have used the cable car.

section.title: Chideock Bypass
section.p: Mr. Letwin: To ask the Secretary of State for the Environment, Transport and the Regions if he will make a statement on the COBA study into options for a Chideock Bypass. [58223]

Ms Glenda Jackson [holding answer 3 November 1998]: No COBA study into options for a Chideock bypass has been carried out. At the 1994 public inquiry into the A35 Chideock/Morcombelake bypass one of the alternatives proposed by objectors was a single carriageway bypass for Chideock alone. The Highways Agency assessed the cost of this scheme as £5.9 million with a COBA net present value of £0.7 million at low traffic growth and £3.7 million at high traffic growth. But this scheme was not considered to represent a viable bypass for the village. An estimate was made by the Highways Agency in 1997 that a single carriageway bypass with climbing lanes for Chideock would cost approximately £12.5 million.

section.title: Teesside Development Corporation
section.p: Dr. Kumar: To ask the Secretary of State for the Environment, Transport and the Regions what happened to the (a) general furniture and (b) boardroom furniture which belonged to Teesside Development Corporation after the demise of the Corporation in April. [58303]
Mr. Meale: I understand that the Corporation's furniture was sold as part of a packaged disposal of its office equipment during its final three-month period.

section.title: Leasehold Reform
section.p: Mrs. Lait: To ask the Secretary of State for the Environment, Transport and the Regions, pursuant to his answer of 31 March 1998, Official Report, column 493, when he expects that the Green Paper on leasehold reform will be published. [58473]
Mr. Raynsford: We hope to issue our consultation paper on leasehold reform shortly.

section.title: Buses (London)
section.p: Mr. Corbyn: To ask the Secretary of State for the Environment, Transport and the Regions what review is being undertaken by his Department of the performance of bus franchises in London; and if he will make a statement. [58226]

Ms Glenda Jackson: The performance of bus passenger services in London is a matter for London Transport. The Department receives regular reports of the overall performance on the bus network and monitors this against targets set by the Secretary of State.

I would refer my hon. Friend to the Government's White Paper "A Mayor and Assembly for London" in which we have said that the present arrangements work well but that Transport for London should be free to develop and improve these arrangements working within a statutory framework similar to the present one.

section.title: Private Cars (London)
section.p: Mr. Corbyn: To ask the Secretary of State for the Environment, Transport and the Regions when he expects to announce detailed proposals on the reduction of private car traffic in central London. [58227]

Ms Glenda Jackson: The Government will be giving the Mayor of London the responsibility and the powers to deal with strategic traffic issues in the capital. The Mayor will produce an integrated transport strategy for London. Boroughs will be required to produce local implementation plans to give effect to this. Meanwhile the Government are promoting initiatives in London to improve public transport and encourage use of modes other than the private car—in line with our White Paper 'A New Deal for Transport'.

section.title: Climate Change Conference
section.p: Mr. Corbyn: To ask the Secretary of State for the Environment, Transport and the Regions if he will make a statement on the aspects of policy covered by the Government's obligation to the Buenos Aires climate change conference to be held in November. [58229]

Mr. Meacher: My right hon. Friend the Deputy Prime Minister will be making a statement to the Buenos Aires Climate Change Conference (COP4) on Thursday 12 November. He will urge that as much progress as possible is made on outstanding implementation, questions of the Kyoto Protocol at COP4 and agreement on a work plan for early resolution of remaining issues. He will also update the Conference on progress made by
643 the United Kingdom Government in meeting its own commitments as set out in the consultation paper 'UK Climate Change Programme', which was issued on 26 October.

Mr. Corbyn: To ask the Secretary of State for the Environment, Transport and the Regions if he will list the delegation he is sending to the Buenos Aires climate convention to be held in November. [58230]

Mr. Meacher: The UK delegation for the Fourth Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change will consist of my right hon. Friend the Deputy Prime Minister, myself and the right hon. Member for Suffolk, Coastal (Mr. Gummer) and a total of 26 officials from the Departments of the Environment, Transport and the Regions, Trade and Industry, International Development and the Foreign and Commonwealth Office.

section.title: Coaches (London)
section.p: Mr. Fearn: To ask the Secretary of State for the Environment, Transport and the Regions what estimate he has made of the current volume at London coach terminals of passengers in transit to locations outside London. [58673]

Ms Glenda Jackson: Coach services interchange at several locations in London including Victoria Coach Station, Bulleid Way, Heathrow Airport, King's Cross and Russell Square. The Government do not compile information about these services. However, I understand it is estimated that around 3 million passengers departing from Victoria Coach Station each year transfer from other coach services at the Station.

section.title: Airline Subsidies
section.p: Mr. Fearn: To ask the Secretary of State for the Environment, Transport and the Regions what (a) legal and (b) diplomatic steps he is taking to stop European Union countries providing state subsidies to national airlines. [58474]

Ms Glenda Jackson: Application of the rules in the Treaty of Rome which govern state subsidies to national airlines is a matter for the European Commission. The UK Government oppose in principle all such subsidies which distort competition in the European single aviation market, and takes advantage of the limited rights granted to Member States under the Treaty, and of appropriate diplomatic opportunities, to present its views. The Commission now assesses requests for state aid more stringently than it did previously, and, when authorising aid to Alitalia in 1997, stated that it did not expect there to be any further such cases.

section.title: Councillors
section.p: Ms Harman: To ask the Secretary of State for the Environment, Transport and the Regions (1) if he will place in the Library the replies to the letters to local authorities asking them how many of their councillors are (a) men and (b) women; [58362]
(2) how many councillors for each local authority are (a) men and (b) women; [58363]
(3) what percentage of all local authority councillors are women; which council has the highest percentage of women councillors; and which has the lowest. [58364]
Mr. Raynsford: Research carried out by the publishers of the Municipal Year Book in the summer indicates that approximately 26 per cent. of councillors in the UK are female.

The replies to the letters to local authorities to which my right hon. Friend refers are not held by this Department. The question of these being placed in the Library is a matter for the Minister for Women and I have asked her to write to my right hon. Friend on this subject.

section.title: African Elephants
section.p: Mr. Burgon: To ask the Secretary of State for the Environment, Transport and the Regions what was the outcome of the third dialogue meeting between African elephant range states held in Arusha, Tanzania from 28 September to 2 October; and if he will make a statement. [58949]

Mr. Meacher: As part of a continuing dialogue, African elephant range states met recently at Arusha to discuss implementation of decisions made at last year's CITES Conference to transfer the elephant populations of Botswana, Namibia and Zimbabwe to Appendix II of the CITES Convention to enable limited trade in elephant products to resume. The UK and other contributors to the costs of the meeting, the European Commission, the USA and Japan, attended as observers.

The 1997 Conference decisions set a number of conditions that have to be met before an experimental one off transhipment of ivory from the three proponent states to Japan can go ahead next year. These include the establishment of new pan-African and Asian monitoring systems to assess the level of elephant poaching and illegal trade in ivory. The World Conservation Union (IUCN) and TRAFFIC (the wildlife trade monitoring arm of IUCN and the World Wide Fund for Nature) were charged with developing these systems. Their proposals were presented to the Arusha meeting and endorsed by the range states present.

While African range states indicated their readiness to help finance the monitoring systems, there will be a need for external funding to get them up and running. Since effective monitoring systems will be vital to informing decision makers on whether the tenth Conference decisions have any adverse effect on levels of poaching and illegal trade, I am today pledging $40,000 of UK support for the new system to monitor illegal trade in ivory. This will enable the system to be set up and provide sufficient resources to fund its first year of operation.

The tenth Conference decisions also addressed the problem of growing Government stockpiles of ivory derived from management programmes and seizures. Parties agreed that fully audited stocks should be taken out of the system by way of non-commercial disposal. In return donors would provide financial assistance for 646 elephant conservation and community development programmes with all monies managed under Conservation Trust Funds. At Arusha, the fourteen African countries that have had their registered government stockpiles audited by TRAFFIC discussed the best way to proceed. They agreed to co-operate in seeking financial assistance for conservation by this means and to route any indications of interest through the CITES Secretariat.

In keeping with this spirit of co-operation and in the expectation that this will lead to offers from other donors, including conservation organisations, I am today writing to the CITES Secretariat to let them know that the UK is willing to contribute £60,000 to fund conservation work in return for disposal of part of the registered ivory stockpile.

section.title: Computer Systems
section.p: Mr. Stringer: To ask the Secretary of State for Social Security what plans he has to modernise the Department's computer systems; and if he will make a statement. [58761]

Mr. Timms: Modernisation of the Welfare State is a priority for the Government and will involve major changes over a period of time to the ways in which welfare services are delivered. A key element of the strategy for the future is to provide the next generation of computer systems required to support improved service delivery to the public, whilst at the same time reducing the scope for error or fraud.

The ACcess to CORporate Data (ACCORD) procurement project was created to put in place Information System/Information Technology (IS/IT) supply arrangements with the private sector. The procurement, conducted in accordance with Government and EC procurement regulations, set out to establish Private Finance Initiative/Public Private Partnership (PFI/PPP) arrangements with suitable service providers.

First of all, in order to develop the core systems for the new IS/IT, the Department is announcing today that it intends to establish a close, long-term working relationship with a single preferred Service Provider. The AFFINITY consortium (led by Electronic Data Systems Ltd. with IBM UK Ltd., Cable and Wireless Communications Ltd. and PricewaterhouseCoopers) has been selected for this role and they will start work with the Department immediately to do the preparatory work necessary to design the strategic components of the next generation of IS/IT.

The Department is also announcing that it has selected three service providers it intends to work with for the provision of a wide range of IS/IT services in the future. As well as the AFFINITY consortium these will be: ARCWAY, a consortium led by British Telecommunications plc with Bull Information Systems Ltd. and SEMA Group UK Ltd.; and 1ACCORD, a consortium led by ICL plc with Anderson Consulting, Experian Ltd., Microsoft Ltd., Rand Information Systems Ltd. and Ferret Information Systems Ltd.
These selections are essential prerequisites to the detailed negotiations which will allow the commercial arrangements to be finalised with the service providers.
Following this, as supply needs arise from now and over the next 10 years, contracts for specific IS/IT services will be awarded through these providers.

We believe this arrangement between public and private provision is an important step towards modernising the Welfare State. In particular the establishing of a strategic relationship and joint working arrangements with the Preferred Service Provider will enable us to harness together the skills from both sectors.

section.title: Pensioner to Working Age Ratio

section.title: Occupational Pension Schemes
section.p: Mr. Derek Twigg: To ask the Secretary of State for Social Security if he will make a statement about the funding of age-related rebates in respect of members of contracted-out money purchase schemes. [58762]

Mr. Denham: Employers who operate contracted-out occupational pension schemes provide their employees with a pension to replace the pension they would have got had they remained in the State Earnings Related Pension Scheme (SERPS).

In contracted-out occupational schemes, both employer and employee pay lower rate National Insurance Contributions in recognition that full SERPS will not be paid. In a Contracted-Out Money Purchase Scheme (COMPS) part of the rebate is deducted from the national insurance contributions due by the employer. The remainder, known as the age-related rebate, is paid by the Contributions Agency to the pension scheme in the tax year following that in which it is due.

Section 42A of the Pension Schemes Act 1993 (PSA) provides the legislative authority for the age related rebate to be paid by the Secretary of State for Social Security to the pension scheme. This section was inserted into the PSA by the Pensions Act 1995. The intention is that these payments should be funded directly from the National Insurance Fund and classed as revenue forgone. However, the necessary provision to facilitate funding in this manner was erroneously omitted from the Pensions Act. So while there is a legislative duty to make the payments, there is no authority to fund them from the National Insurance Fund. As result a number of ultra vires payments have been made from the National Insurance Fund totalling around £490,000 which will have to be refunded from money voted by Parliament.

An amendment to the PSA to correct this defect will be put before Parliament. This will allow the payments to be funded properly from the National Insurance Fund in accordance with the original intention. Until the provisions are enacted temporary arrangements are necessary to ensure that the payments can continue to be made. Provision will also be made to ensure that the National Insurance Fund reimburses those accounts responsible for funding the payments up to the time when the legislation was brought into force.

Legislation under s177(1) of the PSA does, by default, allow the payments to be paid from money provided by Parliament. Since Parliament did not envisage using provision in this way the ambits of the DSS Votes do not cover age related rebates. A Supplementary Estimate is therefore needed to extend the ambit of Class XII, Vote 2. A token Supplementary Estimate of £1,000 has been sought on Vote 2 to amend the ambit to enable payments, totalling £82 million, to be made to Contracted-Out Money Purchase Schemes in respect of age related rebates. As the Contributions Agency computer system, NIRS2, does not have the functionality to separate the payments in respect of age related rebates, which are paid in conjunction with personal pensions, Vote 2 will, therefore, also be responsible for paying personal pensions. The National Insurance Fund which does have the legislative power to pay personal pensions will refund Vote 2 for the payments made on its behalf. These arrangements will continue until the defective legislation is corrected. An advance of £77 million has been sought from the Contingencies Fund to finance urgent expenditure. The advance will be repaid from Vote 2 when Parliament has approved the necessary token Supplementary Estimate.

section.title: Prisons (Quantum Project)
section.p: Ms Moran: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department what progress is being made on the Prison Service Quantum Project. [58941]

Mr. George Howarth: On 10 August 1998, the Director General of the Prison Service called a temporary halt to the Quantum Project and set up a thorough review which will take up to six months. In a message to Prison Service staff he said: "It has become apparent that it may not be possible to achieve the original objectives of providing the Service with improved information systems and business processes in a way which safeguards the vital operational capability of the Service".

These and other concerns will be addressed in the review process, which will reassess the way forward and consider a range of alternative options. The objective is to ensure that the project meets the needs of the Prison Service.

section.title: Police (Objectives)
section.p: Ms Moran: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department what objectives he will be determining for policing for 1999–2000. [58942]

Mr. Straw: I will announce my objectives, which identify our Ministerial priorities for policing in 1999–2000, together with supporting Key Performance Indicators, tomorrow, 6 November. I will arrange for copies to be placed in the Library at 10.00 am.

section.title: Asylum Seekers
section.p: Ms Moran: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department what arrangements are being made to issue monthly statistics of asylum. [58943]

Mr. Straw: Until now, the asylum statistics have been available only in the Home Offices' annual Asylum Statistics Bulletin and in a summary form twice a year in the Control of Immigration Statistical Bulletin. These Bulletins contain detailed information on asylum applications, demographic characteristics of asylum seekers, decisions, appeals, detention and removals.

Selected monthly information has, however, been available only on request from the Home Office Press Office. I am therefore arranging for selected monthly statistics of asylum to be placed on the Home Office Research Development Statistics Website (http://www.homeoffice.gov.uk/rds/index.htm) on the 25th of each month, or the next working day, and to be also available through the Library and the Home Office Press Office.

The proportion of applicants recognised as refugees and granted asylum shows little variation between 1993 and 1996. The increase to 11 per cent. in 1997 reflects grants to Somali and Federal Republic of Yugoslavia nationals. In the first nine months of 1998, the proportion has increased further to 17 per cent. This is partly due to changes made in 1998 so that deserving cases are recognised earlier in the process. The Home Office is continually reassessing the situation in each country in the context of the 1951 United Nations Convention relating to the Status of Refugees and its associated 1967 protocol.

Mr. Clappison: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department what is the timetable of the Youth Justice Board for ending the remand of 15 and 16 year olds to adult prisons. [58355]

Mr. Boateng: The Government's plans for ensuring that appropriate arrangements are in place for remanded juveniles are being taken forward in the context of the wider programme of work arising from our review of all forms of secure accommodation for young offenders and young people held on remand. Our aim is to implement provisions in the Crime and Disorder Act 1998 as soon as possible, and by June 1998 at the latest, to allow the courts to remand directly to local authority secure accommodation 12–14 year olds, 15 and 16 year old girls and, where a place has been identified in advance, vulnerable 15 and 16 year old boys. We will keep under review the existing arrangements for remanding other 15 and 16 year old boys to Prison Service accommodation.

In the meantime, work is being taken forward, with the Youth Justice Board, to improve the standard of care and quality of regimes for remanded and sentenced juveniles held in Prison Service accommodation to ensure that these are appropriate to the needs of young people. We are also making available funds, which will be administered by the Youth Justice Board, to develop local bail support provision to help ensure that custodial remands are used appropriately for the most serious and persistent cases.

section.title: Police (World Cup)
section.p: Mr. Hinchliffe: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department (1) what is the total sum received or to be received by police forces in England and Wales from the Football Association to cover the cost of travel, overseas allowances and overtime in connection with the policing of World Cup matches involving the England team; [58489]

(2) how much in total the Government plan to contribute towards the 24-hour manning of the National Criminal Intelligence Service Football Unit during the World Cup Finals and the costs associated with the provision of football intelligence officers during matches involving the England team. [58490]

Mr. Boateng: The Football Association has met the cost of travel, overseas allowances and overtime for officers from England and Wales. Salary costs have been met by the officers' respective forces. The Football Association also contributed to the cost of relevant police equipment.

The Government agreed to contribute to the costs associated with the 24-hour manning of the National Criminal Intelligence Service during the Finals: and to contribute part of the cost associated with the provision of additional football intelligence officers in France for some England matches. Detailed information about actual costs incurred is operationally sensitive.

section.title: Ethnic Minorities
section.p: Mr. Cox: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department (1) what is the current amount of section 11 funding made available by his Department to the Greater London area; [57909]
(2) if he will make a statement on his Department's future policy towards section 11 funding for the Greater London area. [57763]

Mr. George Howarth: Allocations of Home Office section 11 grant for the 1998–99 financial year to local authorities, grant maintained schools and further education colleges in the Greater London area amount to £34.496 million. Nationally, over 97 per cent. of section 11 grant is currently paid to education projects. It has been decided that, from April 1999, responsibility for such funding should rest with the Department for Education and Employment. A further announcement will be made shortly about the administrative arrangements. The Home Office intends to operate a new grant programme to fund projects in fields other than education. The Department is currently consulting interested parties about the design of this new programme, and a further announcement will be made in due course.

section.title: Immigration
section.p: Mr. Malins: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department how many cases were considered for enforcement under immigration legislation for each year for which figures are known since 1993; and how many deportations were made. [57757]

Mr. George Howarth: The available information, relating to the numbers of cases for which enforcement action was initiated under sections 3(5), 3(6) or 33(1) of the Immigration Act 1971, since 1993; and the number of deportations made, is given in tables 7.2 (Illegal entrants) and 7.4 (Deportation action) of the Home Office Command Paper "Control of Immigration: Statistics United Kingdom 1997" (Cm 4033), for years 1993 and 1994, and in tables 5.1 (Total enforcement action), 5.2 (Illegal entrants) and 5.3 (Deportation action) of the Home Office statistical bulletin "Control of Immigration: Statistics United Kingdom, First Half 1998", issue 24/98, for years 1995–97. Copies of these publications are available in the Library.

section.title: Channel Islands
section.p: Sir Teddy Taylor: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department if he will make a statement on the extent to which European legislation, directives and decisions are enforced upon the Channel Islands and the extent to which the situation has changed since the passing of Protocol 3 to the Treaty of Rome. [57753]

Mr. George Howarth: Protocol 3 to the Treaty of Accession sets out the limited extent to which European Union instruments apply to the Channel Islands and the Isle of Man. The normal practice is for relevant European provisions to be given effect in the Islands through local legislation.
Sir Teddy Taylor: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department what recent representations he has received from the EU Commission relating to the Channel Islands. [57755]
Mr. George Howarth: No recent representations have been received from the European Commission relating to the Channel Islands.

section.title: Criminal Injuries Compensation
section.p: Mr. Waterson: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department if he will review the procedures surrounding the payment of criminal injuries compensation. [58189]

Mr. Boateng: The procedures surrounding the payment of criminal injuries compensation are regularly reviewed within the Criminal Injuries Compensation Authority (CICA)—the body which administers the tariff-based scheme introduced with effect from 1 April 1996—as part of the normal management process. There are no plans to undertake any special procedural reviews at this time.

section.title: Alcohol Consumption (Public Places)
section.p: Mr. Waterson: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department how local authorities and other agencies could be encouraged, perhaps by changes in the law, to deal more effectively with the problems of street drinking. [58196]

Mr. George Howarth: The Home Office encourages local authorities to adopt, whenever appropriate, a model byelaw which makes it an offence to consume intoxicating liquor in a designated place after being warned by a constable not to do so. We have also implemented the Confiscation of Alcohol (Young Persons) Act 1997, which enables a constable to confiscate alcohol being drunk or intended to be drunk in public by someone who is under-age.

The Anti-Social Behaviour Order and other provisions in the Crime and Disorder Act 1998 will help with specific local problems. Local authorities and the police, with their partners, can include any such problems in the crime and disorder audit which is required under the Act and then go on to develop appropriate strategies for tackling this as part of their overall crime reduction strategy.

section.title: Police Manpower
section.p: Mr. Letwin: To ask the Secretary of State for the Home Department how many police officers on the beat there were in (a) May 1997, (b) May 1998 and (c) September 1998. [58251]

Mr. Boateng: Information on the deployment of police personnel is collected annually by Her Majesty's Inspectorate of Constabulary. The number of officers on patrol duties in England and Wales is set out in the table:

section.title: Remploy
section.p: Mr. Rooney: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Employment (1) what discussions his Department has held with Remploy on its corporate plan; [58419]
(2) what role there will be for Remploy employees and their representatives in drawing up Remploy's corporate plan; [58420]
(3) what discussions his Department has held with Remploy on factory closures; [58421]
(4) what variations to Remploy's targets for 1997–98 have been made for the years (a) 1998–99 and (b) 1999–2000; [58422]
(5) what is the forecast subsidy to Remploy in (a) 1999–2000, (b) 2000–01 and (c) 2001–02; [58452]
(6) when he last met the relevant trade unions to discuss the future operations of Remploy. [58453]

Ms Hodge: I understand that Remploy management meet with the Remploy Consortium of Unions at the National Joint Consultative Committee regularly to discuss a range of issues. In particular, Remploy delivered a series of presentations/discussions in July this year to managers and local shop stewards about the strategy set out in the latest Corporate Plan. In addition, national trade union officers received a presentation in May, in advance of the publication of the plan. Remploy intend to adopt a similar approach next time round, and employees have been invited to put forward questions on future strategy and on how they could be more closely involved in planning Remploy's future.
I am expecting Remploy to submit their next Corporate Plan (covering the 3 years 1999–2000 to 2001–02) shortly, for my approval. I will be discussing it with the Remploy Chairman as usual.

Remploy has agreed a broad strategy with Ministers to improve employer opportunities for disabled people both in factories and through Interwork. As part of their strategy Remploy needs to address overcapacity in their factory network through mergers, changes of trade and factory rationalisation. Details of this strategy have been
657 published in Remploy's Corporate Plan for 1998–99 to 2000–01, and in the Remploy booklet "Planning for our Future", issued to Remploy employees. The operational detail involved in implementing this strategy is a matter for the Remploy Board, as it has to be based on commercial decisions which only Remploy can take.

Remploy's targets for 1999–2000 have not yet been agreed. The following variations were agreed with Remploy for 1998–99 in comparison with 1997–98: average number of disabled people—extra 250; average number of Interworkers—extra 350; progressions—extra 50; operating deficit per disabled worker—decrease of £300 per annum (at cash prices); operating deficit per Interworker—decrease of £100 per annum (at cash prices).

Remploy is currently developing its plans for 1999–2000 and for future years. The subsidy will be subject to those plans and further negotiations with the Department. My predecessor, my hon. Friend the Member for Newport, East (Mr. Howarth), met the Remploy unions on 2 February 1998. I intend to meet the Remploy unions myself in due course.

section.title: Careers Service
section.p: Mr. Willis: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Employment what plans he has to require Careers Service contractors to meet an externally verified quality framework if they are to become preferred suppliers under the future contracting arrangements for the Careers Service. [56209]

Mr. Mudie: The Careers Service future contracting is being considered. We are currently considering a number of options and I expect to make an announcement on the future contracting arrangements early in the new year.

section.title: Class Sizes
section.p: Mr. Maclean: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Employment what arrangements are in place for monitoring progress towards meeting the Government's targets on class sizes. [57510]

Ms Estelle Morris [holding answer 2 November 1998]: In addition to the monitoring information available from the Schools' Census data collected each January, we will also be taking a count of infant pupils and classes in September 1999, September 2000 and September 2001.

section.title: Specialist Disability Services
section.p: Mr. Field: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Employment how many of the million people with disabilities cited in Support for Disabled People who state they wish to work will benefit from the investment in specialist disability services announced in this document. [58133]

Ms Hodge [holding answer 3 November 1998]: The Government's recent announcement set out action already taking place and proposed changes to help one million disabled people who are not in work but who want to work. This includes the reform of the All Work Test to focus on capacity as well as incapacity; a single gateway interview to provide advice and support into work; and, looking at ways of helping disabled people stay in work through the New Deal for Disabled People.

Our investment of an additional £30m in specialist disability services will be of direct help to some 8,500 disabled people who need extra support to get a job. Since some of this money will be used to test new ways of helping disabled people into work, the actual number helped over time will be greater.

People with a disability or long term illness will also be able to benefit from the New Deal for Disabled People for which £195 million has been set aside for the lifetime of this Parliament. This will pilot a range of initiatives to help disabled people and those with long-term illness into work and training through the Government's Welfare to Work approach.

section.title: National Childcare Strategy
section.p: Mrs. May: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Employment (1) what estimate his Department has made of the cost to local education authorities of carrying out the audit of supply of, and demand for, childcare required under the National Childcare Strategy; [57698]
(2) what money has been made available to local education authorities to carry out audits of the supply of, and demand for, childcare, as required under the National Childcare Strategy. [57700]

Ms Hodge: I refer the hon. Member to the answer given to her by my hon. Friend the Member for Newport, East (Mr. Howarth) on 16 July 1998, Official Report, column 301. I can confirm that £12 million has now been made available to help local partnerships conduct audits and draw up local childcare plans.

section.title: "Partners in Europe"
section.p: Mr. Laurence Robertson: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Employment how many (a) solicited and (b) unsolicited copies of the schools pack "Partners in Europe" were distributed; and how many remain in stock. [58030]

Mr. Mudie: The information and resource pack for schools "Partners in Europe" was distributed in January 1998 to all schools in the UK on the following basis: two to each school in England, one to each school in Scotland, two to each school in Wales and two to each school in Northern Ireland. Each country was responsible for its own distribution. Copies were also sent to LEAs in England, Scotland and Wales, Education and Libraries Boards in Northern Ireland and organisations such as the Central Bureau for Educational Visits and Exchanges, the Qualifications and Curriculum Authority and OFSTED. Since the initial distribution, there have been 614 requests in England for additional copies. 432 resource packages are currently in stock, but this figure includes the resource pack that was distributed to youth groups in the UK.

Mr. Laurence Robertson: To ask the Secretary of State for Education and Employment what were the (a) printing, (b) preparation and (c) distribution costs of the schools pack "Partners in Europe". [58029]

Mr. Mudie: The costs of producing the 66,000 copies of the schools pack "Partners in Europe" were shared between the four UK education departments and the Foreign and Commonwealth Office. The costs were as
659 follows: (a) printing of specially commissioned booklets and wallets, £129,140; (b) other preparation costs, £66,197, and (c) initial distribution costs, £113,947.

section.title: Judiciary (Training)
section.p: Mrs. May: To ask the Minister of State, Lord Chancellor's Department if the training for the judiciary on the implications of the Human Rights Bill [Lords] will include training relating to (a) equality and (b) disability issues. [57697]

Mr. Hoon: Judicial training is the responsibility of the Judicial Studies Board (JSB) which is an advisory non-departmental public body. The Equal Treatment Advisory Committee of the Board considers all aspects of equal treatment training for the judiciary, including training on increasing awareness of the needs of people with disabilities.

The JSB is currently drawing up the programme of training for full and part-time members of the judiciary in the months prior to implementation of the Human Rights Bill. This will include training on those parts of the European Convention on Human Rights that relate to equality and disability issues.

section.title: Civil Servants (Ethnic Minorities)
section.p: Mr. Vaz: To ask the Minister of State, Lord Chancellor's Department (1) if he will provide a breakdown, in numerical and percentage terms, of the ethnic origin of civil servants in his private office, as at 1 October 1997; [56795]
(2) if he will provide a breakdown, in numerical and percentage terms, of the ethnic origin of civil servants in his Department, by grade, as at 1 October 1997. [56793]
Mr. Hoon: I refer my hon. Friend to the answers given him today by my right hon. Friend the Minister for the Cabinet Office, Official Report, columns 666–71.

section.title: Fishing (Controls)
section.p: Mr. Todd: To ask the Minister of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food what plans he has to introduce new controls over landings into the United Kingdom following the publication of consultative proposals issued on 3 March; and if he will make a statement. [58952]

Mr. Morley: From 5 January 1999 it will be a condition of UK fishing vessel licences that at least four hours notice must be given of all landings of whitefish and shellfish by vessels of 20m overall length and above. Landings (discharge of catches) must then be completed within four hours unless otherwise authorised. These requirements will not, however, apply where landings are made into designated ports during specified hours provided the master or his representative submits a copy of a completed logsheet prior to the discharge of catch taking place. The designated ports will be those set out in the consultation paper issued last March although for a number of ports the specified hours of landing have been changed in response to representations received. Prior notification is already required for the landing of the main pelagic species and this will continue to operate.
These arrangements will be kept under review and, if circumstances alter, changes in the arrangements will be considered.

The new arrangements will be consistent with tougher Community controls on landings currently being finalised and expected to operate from 1 January 1999. These will enable Member States to apply national designated port controls to vessels from other Member States and third countries landing into their territory. A more rigorous control requirement for 4 hours' notice of arrival in port is also expected to apply to vessels landing abroad unless specific designated port arrangements operate.

The Fisheries Departments will be writing to vessels owners and other interests later this month advising them about the detailed arrangements including those for providing prior notification of landing.

section.title: Fishing (Grant Applications)
section.p: Ms Southworth: To ask the Minister of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food if he will make a statement on the charges levied by the Sea Fish Industry Authority when processing applications for grant aid. [58951]

Mr. Morley: The Government intend when the legislative programme allows, to introduce legislation to provide retrospective statutory authority for technical charges levied by the Sea Fish Industry Authority (SFIA) when processing applications for grant aid under the Fisheries Act 1981. This will regularise the position following advice which has cast doubt on the SFIA's view that their powers to charge contained in the Act covered the technical charges which were levied up until 1995.

I believe that the charges levied were reasonable ones and that the costs of making repayments would be disproportionate to any benefit such repayment would confer on those to whom it was made. The Ministry does not therefore propose to meet any claims that are brought before the proposed legislation is in place.

section.title: Genetically Modified Organisms
section.p: Mr. Steen: To ask the Minister of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food what steps he proposes to take to harmonise the current trial procedures of genetically modified crops in the United Kingdom with those carried out in Europe. [56046]

Mr. Rooker [holding answer 3 November 1998]: Controls over the release and marketing of genetically modified organisms (GMOs) are harmonised across the EU by Directive 90/220/EEC. The information requirements to evaluate the safety of GMO releases are set out in this Directive. However, each consent application is reviewed on a case by case basis and trials procedures may vary according to the characteristics of the GMO and the receiving environment.

Furthermore, no genetically modified plant variety may enter tests and trials for National List purposes unless and until a release consent has been issued under the Environmental Protection Act 1990 and the regulations made under it. The UK's National List system implements EU Directives 70/457/EEC and 70/458/EEC which harmonises the requirement to establish that varieties are distinct, uniform and stable (DUS) and, for the main agricultural species, that they have a value for cultivation and use (VCU) before being entered on a National List. The National List system has no role in considering the environmental or human safety aspects of genetic modification.
Mr. Steen: To ask the Minister of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food what plans he has extend the period of tests required for genetically modified seeds; and if he will make a statement. [56047]
Mr. Rooker [holding answer 3 November 1998]: I have no plans to extend the period of tests required for National List purposes.

National List tests and trials are aimed solely at establishing whether candidate varieties are distinct, uniform and stable (DUS) and have value for cultivation and use (VCU) in the UK. The National List system has no role in addressing the environmental or human safety aspects of genetically modification. Genetically modified plant varieties may not enter National List tests and trials unless and until they have the appropriate release consent under the Environmental Protection Act 1990 and the regulations made under it. For most varieties, National List tests and trials normally last two years, though this period may be extended if necessary to provide the required information to establish DUS and VCU.

Mr. Baker: To ask the Minister of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food what plans he has to consult the public on the Supply Chain Initiative for Modification in Agricultural Crops code of practice before it is agreed between Government and industry. [57712]

Mr. Rooker [holding answer 3 November 1998]: The Supply Chain Initiative on Modified Agricultural Crops (SCIMAC) is an industry grouping, which has drawn up guidelines to promote best practice in the growing of genetically modified crops. The Government have welcomed these guidelines as a complement to the statutory controls, but will not give them endorsement until they are satisfied that the industry has implemented measures to secure compliance. It is for the industry to decide what consultations to carry out, and we have impressed upon them the importance of an open and transparent approach.

section.title: BSE
section.p: Dr. Cable: To ask the Minister of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food what estimate he has made of costs incurred to date by Government and other public sector agencies as a result of releasing witnesses for the BSE inquiry. [57084]
Mr. Rooker: No such estimate has been made. The Inquiry has taken evidence from some 60 witnesses who are current members of MAFF and its agencies.
Mr. Levitt: To ask the Minister of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food if the inquiry into BSE is considering the possible role of organophosphates in causing this disease. [57301]
Mr. Rooker: The Inquiry are considering all theories put to them including that relating to the possible role of organophosphates.
Mr. Levitt: To ask the Minister of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food when he expects the current inquiry into BSE to publish its report. [57294]

Mr. Rooker: The Inquiry is due to report to the Minister of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food, the Secretary of State for Health and the Secretaries of State for Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland by 30 June 1999. The Inquiry's report will be published by Government in due course thereafter.
Mr. Dalyell: To ask the Minister of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food if he will make a statement on his Department's responsibility for BSE compensation. [57340]

Mr. Rooker [holding answer 3 November 1998]: Animals suspected of being affected by or exposed to BSE are slaughtered under Section 32 of the Animal Health Act 1981. Under Section 32(3), compensation is payable in respect of the animals slaughtered.

The compensation payable for animals affected by BSE is the market value up to a ceiling of 100% of the indicative market price. The compensation payable for animals suspected of being affected by BSE, but in which the disease is not subsequently confirmed, is the market value of the animal up to a ceiling of 125% of the indicative market price. The indicative market price for the month of November 1998 is £467.
Farmers may also be eligible for payments in relation to exposed animals slaughtered under the Selective Cull, and for offspring animals under the Offspring Cull.

section.title: Meat Inspection Charges
section.p: Mr. Gill: To ask the Minister of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food what representations he has received from the abattoir industry urging meat inspection charges on a headage only basis. [57727]

Mr. Rooker: The Department has received a number of representations calling for the Meat Hygiene Service (MHS) to calculate its charges for hygiene/welfare inspections on a per head basis. The decision for the MHS to calculate its charges on a per-hour basis was taken after full consultation with industry.

section.title: Meat Hygiene Service
section.p: Mr. Gill: To ask the Minister of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food if working knowledge of the English language is a condition of employment for foreign veterinarians engaged by the Meat Hygiene Service. [57726]

Mr. Rooker: Foreign veterinarians engaged by the Meat Hygiene Service are required to have a working knowledge of the English language. The MHS has introduced an assessment, as part of the Official Veterinary Surgeon training course, for non-United Kingdom nationals, to assess their ability to understand and communicate in English.

section.title: Veterinary Service Charges
section.p: Mr. Gill: To ask the Minister of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food what assessment he has made of the impact of additional official veterinary service charges upon the viability of United Kingdom abattoirs. [57723]

Mr. Rooker: The impact on GB abattoirs will depend upon the circumstances prevailing at individual premises. These include the current level of veterinary supervision, the size and throughput of the premises, the complexity and standard of hygiene of operations and the type of animal being slaughtered. The MHS will notify plant operators of the intended arrangements and the charging implications for their plant in advance of any changes being made.

section.title: Farm Income (Currency Mechanisms)
section.p: Mr. Mitchell: To ask the Minister of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food in which of his Department's publications the basis and operation of the ecu basket of currencies and national green currencies used for calculating price support for agricultural products is described; and what assessment he has made of the extent to which these mechanisms influence the net farm income available to farmers in the United Kingdom (a) currently and (b) following the introduction of the euro. [57484]
Mr. Rooker: The precise basis and operation of the current agrimonetary regime is not outlined in any of my Department's publications.

The agrimonetary regime has sheltered farm incomes from the full effect of the strong pound by slowing down the rate at which currency strength feeds through to the sterling value of CAP prices and direct payments. UK farm incomes are also benefiting from the current green rate freeze, which has been worth £400m to UK farmers over the last two years.

The Commission's draft regulations, which are still under discussion, propose a move to daily market rates, but also include measures for 100% EU financed compensation for any cuts in direct payments in 1999. This would cushion the impact of the end of the green rate freeze on UK farm incomes, and has been welcomed by UK farming organisations.

section.title: Beef of the Bone
section.p: Mr. Maclean: To ask the Minister of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food what is (a) the overall cost to date and (b) the average annual cost per farm of deboning beef products as a result of the ban on sales of beef on the bone. [57503]

Mr. Rooker [holding answer 2 November 1998]: Under the Beef Bones Regulations 1997, deboning may take place in the course of a business at any food premises, including farm shops selling meat, before sale to the ultimate consumer. The estimated costs of these controls were set out in the Regulatory Appraisal which
665 accompanied the Regulations when they were presented to Parliament. A copy is available in the Library of the House. No costs were included or are available for deboning beef on farms as these, with the exception of farm shops, are not food premises as defined in the Food Safety Act 1990 where beef can be deboned.

section.title: Piglet Mortality
section.p: Mr. Michael J. Foster: To ask the Minister of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food what estimate he has made of the number of piglets lost annually to predation, and of the economic loss which this represents. [57924]
Mr. Rooker: None. The information necessary to make such estimates is not available centrally.

section.title: Agricultural Prices
section.p: Mr. Waterson: To ask the Minister of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food what additional resources will be allocated to assist farming communities with the fall in produce prices. [58190]

Mr. Rooker: The Government fully appreciate the difficulties currently being faced by all sectors of the farming industry. We are well aware, as a result of discussions with farmers' leaders and visits to rural areas, that many farmers would welcome additional assistance to cope with their current difficulties.

However, given the tight position on public expenditure we must give very careful consideration before extending any package of assistance to farmers. We are keenly aware of the case being put by the farming unions and other interested organisations, and are now considering the options available to us.

section.title: Bovine Tuberculosis
section.p: Mr. Webb: To ask the Minister of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food what estimate he has made of the percentage of the loss to farmers whose cattle are affected by bovine TB which is covered by the Ministry's compensation scheme; and if he will provide a breakdown of his estimate of the total losses incurred. [58075]

Mr. Rooker: The National Farmers Union estimates the total cost to farmers of tuberculosis in cattle in Great Britain to average £5,300 per animal slaughtered, including consequential losses, although the cost to individual farm businesses varies widely.

During 1997 compensation was paid at 75% of market value of cattle slaughtered as TB reactors, subject to a limit (calculated from the average market price for dairy cattle) which averaged £656 across the year. This represents 12% of £5,300. Since 26 August 1998 compensation has been paid equal to the full market value of slaughtered cattle. To the end of October payments made averaged £970, 18% of £5,300.

section.title: Cattle Blood
section.p: Mr. Letwin: To ask the Minister of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food if he will list the regulations which apply to the transport of blood of cattle over 30 months, following their slaughter. [58246]

Mr. Rooker [holding answer 3 November 1998]: Carriers of waste blood from OTMS animals must register with the Environment Agency or the Scottish Environment Protection Agency under the Controlled Waste (Registration of Carriers and Seizure of Vehicles) Regulations 1991. The only exception relates to the transport of blood from diseased animals, which may be transported by persons who hold an approval or registration under the Animal By-Products Order 1992, and who transport the blood in connection with the activity to which the approval or registration applies. In such cases the Order requires the blood to be collected and transported in suitable containers or vehicles in such a way as to prevent leakage.

section.title: Agricultural Wages Order
section.p: Mr. Maclean: To ask the Minister of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food what is the estimated compliance cost of the most recent agricultural wages order. [58454]

Mr. Rooker: Agricultural wages orders are made by the Agricultural Wages Board which is an independent statutory body. The Board's most recent order, the Agricultural Wages Order 1998 (No. 2) came into effect on 1 October 1998. This order introduced a number of changes to bring the terms of the order into line with the provisions of the Working Time Regulations 1998, which also came into effect on 1 October. The most significant changes introduced were the extension of leave entitlements to casual workers who have been employed by the same employer for 13 weeks, and an entitlement to an unpaid 30 minute rest break.

Information on the compliance costs associated with the implementation of the Working Time Regulations is given in Annexe E to the consultation paper "Measures to Implement Provisions of the EC Directives on the Organisation of Working Time and the Protection of Young People at Work" (URN: 98/645). This was issued by the Department of Trade and Industry in April 1998.
